description: We are an interdisciplinary team passionate about space technology, robotics, AI/ML, engineering, and data-driven problem solving. We combine skills in mechanical design, CAD, programming, AI/ML, electronics, simulation, and research to turn ideas into practical solutions. We are looking for creative, committed teammates who enjoy solving challenging problems, learning new technologies, and building innovative solutions using NASA’s open data.
summary:
We developed ARES-SURVIVOR, an interactive tactical Extravehicular Activity (EVA) operating system and traverse planner for crewed Martian surface exploration. Addressing the "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge, our platform transforms static orbital data into a meter-scale survival suite across Jezero Crater and Gale Crater’s newly discovered 2025 boxwork formations.

The system fuses five NASA scientific domains: HiRISE optical imagery, MOLA topographic elevation, Curiosity RAD radiation flux, CRISM mineralogy, and MEDA meteorology. Central to the platform is a bio-metabolic A* pathfinding engine that penalizes steep grades , regolith slip, and radiation, providing real-time calculations for oxygen consumption, battery draw, and travel duration. We also integrated an interactive 3D WebGL terrain and rover digital twin, live ROS 2 / LiDAR SLAM teleoperation, and an embedded neural network (95.9% accuracy) for instant hazard inference.

ARES-SURVIVOR is vital because global maps lack the physiological awareness and localized fidelity needed for human spacewalks. By unifying orbital intelligence with life-support telemetry across helmet HUD, field tablet, and habitat command modes, our system ensures astronaut survival while accelerating Martian astrobiological discovery.
details:
The Story Behind Our Project

When most people imagine astronauts on Mars, they picture heroic explorers stepping out onto red dust. The reality is much grimmer. Walking on Mars inside a rigid, pressurized spacesuit is exhausting, clumsy, and terrifyingly risky. Your knees and ankles can barely bend, you are breathing from a finite tank on your back, and a single slip down a rocky slope or a patch of hidden, loose sand can end a mission before it even begins.

Global satellite maps are great for scientists sitting comfortably on Earth, but they are practically useless to an astronaut standing on the ground trying to figure out if the ridge fifty feet ahead will cause them to tumble over. That gap is why we built our project, ARES Navigator.

What We Built and How It Works

We wanted to turn cold satellite data into a living, interactive survival copilot for Martian explorers.

Instead of showing a flat map, our software pulls together real NASA images, elevation scans, radiation trackers, and weather reports across famous exploration sites like Jezero Crater and the newly studied boxwork formations in Gale Crater.

The heart of our system is an intelligent pathfinder that cares about human stamina. Typical GPS tools only care about the shortest distance, but on Mars, a straight line can get you killed. Our system constantly checks the steepness of the ground, keeps astronauts away from inclines that are too steep for suit boots, steers around soft dunes that swallow wheels and boots, and calculates exactly how much oxygen and battery life every step will burn.

To make it feel real, we designed three ways to use it:

  • A helmet visor view that puts critical numbers, artificial horizons, and target locks right in front of the astronaut eyes, complete with procedural wind audio based on real Mars microphone recordings.
  • A glove-friendly 3D field tablet where explorers can tilt, rotate, and inspect the terrain in full 3D before taking a single step.
  • A habitat command screen where crew members back at the base station can track their teammate, monitor satellite communication windows, and catalog core samples.

We even linked in an interactive 3D digital twin of a Mars exploration rover, complete with laser radar scanning and simulated live controls, so astronauts can send an autonomous scout ahead before walking into unknown territory.

How We Built It

We wanted everything to run instantly in any web browser without needing expensive supercomputers or slow cloud servers.

We built the core web application using React and TypeScript for rock-solid stability, styled it with Tailwind CSS, and powered the 3D Martian terrain and rover using Three.js and WebGL. This lets anyone fly around hills and craters smoothly at sixty frames per second.

For the robotics and scouting side, we used ROS 2 and the Gazebo simulation engine to test real robotic laser mapping and obstacle avoidance. We also trained a lightweight neural network directly on simulated mobility and slip telemetry. It runs right in the user browser in less than a millisecond, giving astronauts an instant heads-up if the ground beneath them is safe, risky, or hazardous.

The Human Decisions Behind Our Design

Every design choice we made came from putting ourselves in the astronaut boots:

First, we thought about physical fatigue. Walking in a space suit burns immense energy. Climbing even a mild slope dramatically spikes your heart rate and drains oxygen fast. Our system constantly warns explorers before they commit to an uphill climb that might leave them stranded without enough air to walk back.

Second, we tackled the communication delay. Earth is millions of miles away, meaning a simple radio message takes anywhere from five to twenty minutes to reach home. An astronaut standing in front of a sudden drop cannot wait for Houston to reply with permission to take a detour. Everything in our tool runs locally on the spot, giving the crew immediate answers when seconds count.

Finally, we focused on science. Explorers are not just trying to survive; they are on Mars to answer humanity biggest question: was there ever life out there? Our planner deliberately guides routes toward mineral-rich clays, carbonates, and ancient hydrothermal veins, ensuring every step taken is both as safe as possible and scientifically meaningful.

Why This Matters

Going to Mars will be the most daring journey humans have ever attempted. By taking raw satellite numbers and reshaping them into an intuitive, lifelike companion that protects human lungs, joints, and equipment, we hope to build the digital lifeline that helps the first pioneers explore the Red Planet and make it back home safely.
